e11183: Your autonomic nervous system runs three broad modes: safe and social (calm, curious, connected), fight or flight (mobilized, tense, irritable) and shutdown (numb, foggy, heavy). Polyvagal theory (Stephen Porges) is a helpful map for this, though researchers still debate its details. In daily life: the snappy commute, the 3 p.m. slump and the “I can’t open my inbox” freeze are states, not character.
e11184: Set three phone alarms (morning, midday, evening). When each rings, name your state out loud as green, yellow or red, plus one body clue: jaw, shoulders, stomach or breath. Don’t fix anything yet; just notice.

e11190: Needs before growth: Maslow and HALT
e11191: Unmet basics hijack behavior. When sleep, food, safety or belonging are shaky, patience and motivation collapse, and no pep talk fixes that. The quickest daily check is HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired. Before calling yourself (or anyone) lazy, ask which lower need is short.
e11192: Run HALT three times today before reacting to anything. Fix the cheapest item first: eat, drink water, step outside, text a friend, or take a 10-minute rest.

e11197: Fight, flight, freeze, fawn, and your first-aid breath
e11198: Under threat, including criticism and conflict, not just physical danger, your body picks an automatic response: fight (raise your voice), flight (leave, or bury yourself in busyness), freeze (go blank) or fawn (agree quickly to keep the peace). These are survival reflexes, not character flaws. Your starter tool is the physiological sigh: two sharp inhales through the nose, then one long exhale through the mouth.
e11199: Notice your default response in one small friction today (a curt message, a critical comment). Then do 3 physiological sighs at a red light or before opening email.
